text: Each map holds 537 bomb hits. One is pure chance, the other follows a rule. Which is chance? In 1944, Londoners claimed flying bombs fell in clusters, and precise aim would put factories at risk. Build the detector your eye is running. Cut each map into 576 squares, and flag any square with three or more hits, like this one. Map A lights up with 39 targets, map B with none. So A looks aimed. Backwards. I dropped every hit on map A at random, so all 39 targets are false alarms. Map B's rule, no two hits closer than four-fifths of a square. Your eye, like the detector, expects chance to look that even. Each bomb has a one in five 76 chance of landing in this square. To stay empty, all 537 must miss. Guess how many squares stay empty? About 227. Map A has 222. Those empty squares force pileups. The other 354 share all the hits, so 183 must land where another already did. To judge London, chance must predict every bar. Let's call the average hits per square lambda. 1 minus a small slice raised to a big power is e to the minus lambda, almost exactly. Call that P of 0. For two hits in this square, pick two bombs. 537 times 536 ways over 2 since order doesn matter Each has that same chance and the rest miss E to the minus lambda again 536 is almost 537 For three hits each two becomes a three For any k a k The powers merge into lambda to the k, the Poisson distribution. Times 576 squares, it predicts these purple The honest detector compares whole histograms. 39 targets and chance predicts 39. The chi-squared misfit squares each bar's gap and divides by chance's bar. So a miss on a short bar counts more. Map A scores, 2.0. Three out of four simulated chance maps score worse. That share P is .74. Now map B. Map B. Half the expected empty squares, a tower of single hits, misfit 272. A pattern this even is the fingerprint of a spacing rule. Aimed bombs would miss the other way. Extra empty squares, extra pileups. In 1946, R.D. Clark published the same test on London's real hits. 537 in 576 squares. Chance predicted 227 empty squares. Clark counted 229. Overall, P equals 0.88. London's clusters were no sign of precise aim. The bombs were aimed at central London, but tended to fall short so farther north, hits were about half as dense. The test needs one lambda. Clark chose an area where it held steady. The clumps in map A are what no aim at all looks like. If you chose map B, you chose the rule. Thank you.
